lines.text: Most people assume GPS is simple geometry: satellites broadcast their location and your phone triangulates your position.
In truth, if satellite engineers had relied on classical Newtonian physics, your navigation map would drift by over ten kilometers every single day.
Because GPS satellites orbit at nearly four kilometers per second, Einstein's Special Relativity dictates their clocks tick slower, losing seven microseconds a day.
However, twenty thousand kilometers above Earth, gravity is four times weaker, and General Relativity dictates that weaker gravity makes clocks run forty-five microseconds faster.
Subtracting the speed loss from the gravitational gain leaves a net acceleration of thirty-eight microseconds every single day.
Because radio signals travel at the speed of light, thirty-eight microseconds multiplies into eleven point four kilometers of positioning error every twenty-four hours.
To fix this, engineers pre-slowed satellite atomic clocks before launch to ten point two two nine megahertz, so Einstein's universe makes them tick in perfect unison on Earth.
